title: Ranking cloud findings by reachability, permissions and data access, with fix-first plans
problem: Cloud security tools raise more findings than engineers can fix, many with no route to harm, and teams investigate only about 4% of alerts.
approach: Platforms combine reachability, toxic permissions and sensitive-data access into attack paths; Microsoft's invitation-only preview agent produces a ranked, explained action plan.
Findings reach engineers only after validation confirms exploitability, and people decide and act on the agent's plan.
Wiz says more than half of initial high-priority findings were removed once these filters applied (vendor-published).

title: Agent investigates cloud detections, is validated alongside analysts, then closes low-severity alerts
problem: Cloud detections need identity, network, runtime and code context from several consoles, and manual investigation across sprawling environments can take hours.
approach: Wiz's Blue Agent gathers evidence, compares activity with a baseline and gives a verdict; ZS first ran it alongside analysts.
Analysts review what the agent closed at each shift's end, and higher-severity detections stay with analysts.
ZS reports about 95.17% agreement with analysts (self-reported); Owkin reports a 75% cut in false-positive investigation time (vendor-published).

title: In-house cloud triage agent with evidence rules and approval for access changes
problem: At Cohere one critical finding took 30 minutes to 2 hours to investigate; WRITER saw thousands of alerts with roughly 100 truly actionable, about a 2% signal rate.
approach: Cohere built an MCP server so its agent reads Wiz issues, checks duplicate tickets and writes notes back; WRITER built open-source Cerebro.
Cohere analysts start from a populated report and ticket; WRITER requires human approval for IAM and network-boundary changes.
Cohere reports about 145 SecOps hours a week eliminated and attack-path analysis cut to 20 seconds (vendor-published).

title: Combining weak runtime signals with posture context into one critical attack-sequence finding
problem: Individual runtime findings on EC2, ECS and EKS are noisy, and a runtime signal alone often stays below the threshold for a critical finding.
approach: Amazon GuardDuty correlates weak signals into one attack-sequence finding and, from 2026-05-20, attaches vulnerability, reachability, misconfiguration and sensitive-data indicators.
Responders contain exposures, isolate reachable hosts, rotate credentials and patch.
AWS says roughly one in four prioritised runtime-process attack sequences were net-new after the indicators were added (vendor-published).

title: Read-only first-pass incident triage agent across a Kubernetes fleet
problem: First-pass triage of Kubernetes incidents needs pod state, logs, metrics and deployment history from many clusters before a person can act.
approach: A talk abstract describes an open-source agent, one per cluster, doing first-pass triage; the author says it never wrote to a cluster.
Engineers receive the triage and act; the author reports 4 failures in over a year despite read-only permissions (self-reported).

title: Agent finds owner, root cause and fix layer, then drafts the remediation
problem: Security teams often do not know who owns a vulnerable resource or which layer to fix, and Wiz says routing can take longer than the fix itself.
approach: Wiz's Green Agent suggests an owner, traces root cause, gives a Remediate or Ignore verdict and drafts fixes; Orca, CrowdStrike offer similar.
Teams choose whether to open a pull request or send the fix to a coding agent; sensitive systems need approval.
project44 reports 10x faster vulnerability remediation (vendor-published).
who: project44, Wiz, Orca, CrowdStrike, La Centrale

title: Evidence-gated automatic fixing of cloud misconfigurations: safe fixes run, risky await
problem: Tamnoon says teams investigate about 4% of alerts, critical misconfigurations sit unresolved 128 days on average, and human change boards cannot authorise fixes in minutes.
approach: Tamnoon scores findings SAFE, RISKY or UNSAFE: safe fixes run from playbooks, risky ones await approval, unsafe go to the owning team.
Crossmint and Flywire practitioners built custom auto-remediation; high-impact or irreversible actions go to a person.
A research prototype cut change-policy violations to 4.73% against 9.95% for a standard toolchain (independent).

title: AI turns unused-access findings into least-privilege changes delivered as code pull requests
problem: Permissions accumulate, console fixes are overwritten at next deployment, and tightening access can break workflows; 59% of AWS IAM users had a key older than a year.
approach: An AWS daily automation reads Access Analyzer findings and uses Bedrock models to produce a pull request with code and plain-English explanation.
The role-owning team reviews the pull request; at Smolen's pipeline, security reviews AccessDenied-driven pull requests.
No outcome figures are published for the AWS automation or the Smolen pipeline.

title: Multi-agent cloud security team scores identity risk, applies controls and red-teams them
problem: Most security teams have no dedicated cloud identity person, so access clean-up is nobody's priority.
approach: A fwd:cloudsec abstract describes four agents (identity, red team, threat intelligence, behaviour analytics) in a real AWS account with 500+ identities.
Identity agent scored risk and applied controls, a red-team agent checked each control blocked its attack path; approval workflows gate dangerous actions.
The author reports a 42.7% risk score reduction after five days (self-reported).

title: AI-assisted discovery of new cloud privilege-escalation paths, validated in a lab first
problem: Language models surface new attack vectors quickly but also hallucinate issues that are not exploitable, which wastes researcher time.
approach: An agentic workflow pairs AI-driven discovery with deterministic integration tests in an open-source lab, so every candidate is validated before publication.
The researcher decides what to publish after tests pass.
The speaker reports over a dozen new AWS privilege-escalation paths found and validated (self-reported).

title: Guardrails and independent checks for AI-written infrastructure code
problem: AI assistants now write most infrastructure code in many organisations, and valid Terraform is not necessarily secure; repairs can satisfy a scanner while leaving the flaw.
approach: A reference architecture has an MCP server expose approved Terraform modules, run policy checks, auto-fix eligible violations and open a pull request.
High-risk exceptions go to humans, and destructive changes land as pull requests for review.
Independent research found 71.4% of plan-compared LLM repairs of Terraform misconfigurations were deceptive (independent).

title: Idea: agents detect drift from infrastructure code and propose reconciling updates
problem: Idea, not a deployment: when consoles and scripts are used alongside infrastructure code, deployed systems drift from the specification and later runs may undo valid changes.
approach: Idea from research: agents read API traces to detect out-of-band change and propose infrastructure code updates, with a verifier agent.
Human checkpoints are not described; engineer review before merge is inferred.
Research prototypes report drift reconciliation accuracy of 0.71 to 0.97 (independent).

title: Virtual patching at the firewall and network layer, with AI-assisted rules
problem: Patching takes weeks (a 43-day median for critical flaws is cited), and tuning web firewall rules across hundreds of technology stacks does not scale with headcount.
approach: An Adobe manager's talk abstract describes AI-assisted rule generation and tuning in a human-in-the-loop pipeline; Palo Alto Networks announced network-level virtual patches.
Humans approve rules; the abstract claims a capability of going from 43 days to single-digit minutes (self-reported claim).
who: Adobe (speaker), Palo Alto Networks, IBM, Red Hat

title: AI firewall policy hygiene: flagging stale, overly permissive and conflicting rules
problem: Firewall rulebases grow through temporary exceptions and cloud deployments, and Check Point says policies become risky after months of change, with reviews waiting for the next cycle.
approach: Cato Networks' announced agent compares rule behaviour with traffic and flags forgotten and overly permissive rules; Check Point finds redundant, conflicting rules.
Administrators select which recommended rules to apply; no outcome figures are published.

title: AI turns firewall intent into rules, with change-impact checks grounded in topology
problem: Firewall change-impact analysis used to come from outside tools, and language models translate intent well but miss policy violations when not grounded in topology.
approach: Fortinet, Palo Alto Networks, Check Point and Cisco announced features that take an intent, write a rule and report its effect.
The change board signs the change, and human approval or a policy check precedes any AI-initiated network change.
A research prototype cut missed policy violations by over 30% (independent); no vendor adoption figures are published.
who: Fortinet, Palo Alto Networks, Check Point, Cisco

title: Runtime guardrails and telemetry for coding agents on developer endpoints
problem: Coding agents act on privileged developer endpoints, users switch approvals off, and an agent can cause an incident without malicious input.
approach: Perplexity open-sourced Numbat, which hooks into coding agents, enforces rules, records activity and sends telemetry; a scheduled agent proposes tested detection changes.
Rule changes the agent proposes go through human-reviewed pull requests.
It runs on thousands of Perplexity endpoints, with no detection-quality figures published (self-reported).

title: Idea: AI agents tune endpoint detection policy from a bounded catalogue
problem: Idea, not a deployment: commercial endpoint detection now includes autonomous AI parts, so an agent tuning it acts on a black box that can change its own behaviour.
approach: Idea from research: an LLM agent selects hardening actions from a finite, tool-enforced catalogue, tested in a lab against a commercial product.
A prototype cut the attacker's expected payoff 59% against a greedy baseline (independent); human checkpoints are not described.

title: AI-assisted cloud detection engineering, with testing that catches hallucinated log fields
problem: Detection engineers must write and maintain rules across cloud telemetry as threats change, and one AWS rule sat in a production SIEM nine months without firing.
approach: Wiz and Cloudflare postings list AI use for detection and log analysis; a Meta engineer's open-source analyser checks rule fields against schemas.
Detection researchers own and review rules.
The Meta engineer found significant quality defects in 1 in 3 cloud detection rules in two public repositories (self-reported).

title: Idea: agents run attack simulations in sandboxes to map telemetry to techniques
problem: Idea, not a deployment: cloud detection engineering is hobbled by poor telemetry documentation and vague, static mappings from log entries to attack techniques.
approach: Idea from a conference abstract: agents run attack call graphs in sandbox accounts on three clouds and record which telemetry actually fires.
Detection engineers curate the resulting knowledge base; review steps are not described and no results are published.

title: Idea: cloud canaries and deception to detect and steer autonomous AI attackers
problem: Idea, not a deployment: frontier agents can chain attack steps in the cloud, and compromise rate alone says little about whether defenders can see them.
approach: A lab scored 10 models across 599 autonomous attack runs in a hard AWS environment, with canaries and deception present or absent.
Canary hits go to the normal detection and response queue; results and review steps are not in the abstract.

title: Continuous cloud compliance: AI-assisted evidence collection and policy written as code
problem: Point-in-time compliance checks cannot keep pace with dynamic cloud environments, and public-sector teams need AI discovery and remediation inside a FedRAMP High boundary.
approach: Wiz announced on 2026-10-14 its agents are available in its FedRAMP High environment; research turns plain-language policy into executable rules.
Human approval is configurable per workflow for sensitive systems.
A research prototype's rules compiled 95.3% of the time (independent); no figures published for Wiz's agents.

title: Shared security AI platform team on which security functions build governed agents
problem: Each security function wants agents, and Databricks lists high-risk workflows such as offensive personas, untrusted inputs, sensitive data, production access and automated tool execution.
approach: Databricks advertises a team owning a shared platform where security functions build governed agents, covering identity, sandboxing, policy enforcement, auditability and evaluation.
Domain teams own their agents' outcomes; the platform team owns guardrails. This is piloting; CrowdStrike sells a similar product.
No figure for Databricks.

title: Managed cloud security services delivered on a multi-tenant AI security platform
problem: Managed service providers juggle fragmented consoles, client policies and scattered visibility, which slows response as client estates grow.
approach: Wiz announced on 2026-09-28 a provider programme with multi-tenant management, just-in-time provisioning and portfolio dashboards; Optiv, SEP2 and Deloitte are quoted.
Wiz says analysts can review and audit the Blue Agent's investigation and verdict; no outcome figures published.

title: Idea: runtime control layer deciding whether live cloud actions proceed or escalate
problem: Idea, not a deployment: SACR argues cloud security platforms still rely on periodic telemetry and human remediation queues while workloads and AI actions change in seconds.
approach: SACR defines a runtime layer linking platform evidence to a decision to proceed, constrain, remediate or escalate, with audit-grade records.
Escalation sends the action to a person; where that boundary sits was unresolved across CSA's summits.
